analysis.one_liner: Lets workers alleging sexual assault or harassment take employers to court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 335-97 with all 222 voting Democrats and 113 Republicans in favor, the Senate passed it by voice vote, and it became Public Law 117-90 on March 3, 2022.
analysis.plain_summary: Many employers require workers to sign agreements up front saying that if a dispute ever arises, it must be settled by a private arbitrator, not a judge, and that the worker cannot join a class action. This law says that at the choice of the person alleging sexual assault or sexual harassment, such agreements cannot be enforced, so the worker can go to court and can join a class action. It applies to claims arising after March 3, 2022.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers (and class representatives) who allege sexual assault or sexual harassment. Instead of being pushed into a private arbitration process chosen by the employer, they can elect to sue in court, in front of a judge, with public proceedings and appeal rights, and they can join class or collective actions. People making claims under federal, tribal, or state law are all covered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers alleging sexual assault or harassment

how_it_helps.text: A court decides whether the law applies and whether the arbitration agreement is unenforceable — the employer cannot force that question into arbitration itself.
The law strikes down both predispute arbitration agreements and predispute class-action waivers for these disputes, at the election of the person alleging the conduct.
It covers disputes under federal, tribal, or state law, and applies to any claim that arises on or after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that relied on mandatory arbitration clauses and class-action waivers — including large companies and chains — lose a tool that kept these disputes out of court and out of juries. The private arbitration industry loses a stream of cases. Businesses may face more litigation over these claims, including class actions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using forced arbitration and arbitration providers

drawbacks.text: Arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for some claims, and employers lose that option for sexual assault and harassment disputes; business groups and some members sought to narrow the bill's scope, including an amendment on the House floor.

The law is narrow: it leaves forced arbitration intact for every other kind of workplace dispute, such as wage theft, discrimination based on other traits, or retaliation, which still can be sent to arbitration under old rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and targeted: a worker alleging sexual assault or harassment gets the choice of a public courtroom rather than a private process chosen by the employer. The main cost falls on employers and arbitration providers in the form of more court litigation over these specific claims, and the law does nothing about forced arbitration for other kinds of disputes. On balance, the gain to workers is direct and the costs are real but limited.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Judiciary Committee, passed the House 335-97, passed the Senate by voice vote without amendment, and was signed by the President on March 3, 2022.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 16, 2021 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The committee approved it 27-14 on November 17, 2021 and reported it in amended form in January 2022.
The House passed it 335-97, with all 222 voting Democrats in favor and Republicans split 113-97.
During House debate an amendment by Representative Buck was debated and a recorded vote was demanded on it; the bill that became law does not include such a narrowing amendment.
The Senate passed the bill without amendment by voice vote on February 10, 2022.
The President signed it on March 3, 2022, making it Public Law 117-90.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers alleging sexual assault or harassment are better off: they can now choose court over employer-chosen arbitration. Employers and the arbitration industry are worse off, having lost that control.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers who can now sue in court

sides.party_line_note: House passage was 335-97: Democrats voted 222-0 in favor while Republicans split 113-97; the committee vote was 27-14 and the Senate passed the bill by voice vote.

industries.note: These employers can no longer enforce upfront arbitration agreements or class-action waivers for sexual assault and harassment claims, meaning these disputes can reach public courts and juries. Their interest in keeping disputes private ran against workers' ability to sue.
Arbitration providers lose a category of cases that previously could not be taken to court. Their revenue depended on employers' ability to channel disputes into paid arbitration.
